title: Plain Language as an Equity Practice
before: A conversation about writing accurate information people can find, understand and use, and why that is an everyday equity practice.

turns.text: Plain Language as an Equity Practice starts with a sentence many of us have read: “Please complete the applicable process following authorization.” What action does that name? Which document, person or deadline? This course looks at how wording, structure, format and timing affect whether someone can act on information, and why unclear writing quietly shifts the burden onto the reader.

And the course is careful to say what plain language is not. It isn’t less accurate. It helps the intended reader find, understand and use information, with familiar words, clear structure and a visible next step, while keeping the necessary details. Complex ideas can be explained plainly. Changing a requirement to make it sound easier would change the meaning.

The opening practice case shows how a small phrase can matter. A notice explains a service change accurately but says only, “Contact your usual representative.” A first-time reader may not know who that is. Over time, wording like that favors people who already have established contacts. You’ll consider what would actually close the gap in that instruction.

From there, the course offers practical habits. Begin with the reader’s purpose, whether that’s understanding what changes, whether it affects them, or what they can do. Name who can do what, how and when. Separate required steps from options. Define acronyms where they’re needed. And if a detail is still unsettled, say so and point to how to get an update.

Structure carries meaning, too. Headings, short sections, descriptive links and purposeful lists help people find information, and a picture of text may not work with the tools someone uses to read. So readable wording belongs alongside accessible formats, usable timing and language assistance. Plain language is one part of access, not a substitute for the others.

There’s a workplace case I think many people will recognize. A newcomer receives an email: “Send the packet after the usual check.” They ask what it means, and a colleague calls the question a lack of initiative. You’ll work through what a stronger response looks like, and how unexplained shorthand can later be mistaken for weak performance.

The course also addresses tone. A clear message can describe an unavailable option without judging the person who asked for it. It names the relevant condition and the next route, if one exists. Courtesy should support clarity, and a warm opening can’t make up for a question that was never actually answered.

Then there’s reader feedback. In one practice situation, community members understand a program name but can’t tell whether a notice requires them to respond. Staff propose replacing only the longest words. You’ll decide how best to use that feedback. The course also suggests testing an instruction by asking a reader to describe the next step, without turning that into a test of the person.

I appreciated the point about evidence. A revision is an action; a clearer next step is a possible result. Fewer questions alone don’t establish understanding, because people may also stop asking when a route feels unhelpful. And a clearer web page can still conflict with an old attachment or template, so recurring wording may need a consistent correction.

Near the end, you’ll rewrite a practice instruction: “Refer the matter through the normal channel.” You’ll name the action, explain the channel and identify one detail that needs verification. Then you’ll consider what burden the original placed on someone unfamiliar with the process. Clarity is shared work, but the reader shouldn’t have to produce or approve the draft.

As you go, keep a message from your own work in mind, perhaps a notice, an email or an instruction you send often. Read it as someone new to the process would. Is the next step visible? Is anything assumed? Bring that example with you, and see what the practice suggests you might change.

guidance.title: Clear without changing the meaning
guidance.text: Plain language is sometimes mistaken for leaving things out. The aim is the opposite: keep what the reader needs and remove what makes it hard to find. If a requirement has conditions, those conditions stay. If a choice has consequences, the reader should still see them. Ask whether your revision changes what the reader must do, or only how easily they can see it.

guidance.title: Who carries the effort?
guidance.text: Choose one instruction you write or forward regularly. Who reads it, and what do they already need to know to act on it? If someone new to the process received it today, where might they get stuck? Consider who could help you test it, and which parts you could revise while keeping the actual requirements intact.
